en.intro: Today, in an archive reading room. Nia, an archivist, and the Grandson, a man in his forties from the family, lay out the place-name notes behind the story: Cedwyn, Cwm-Cedwyn, Nant-Cedwyn, Ynys-Cedwyn, Cedfin, Cydfin, Cydwin and Tŷ Mawr, the Great House. They sort what each note rests on, what is catalogued and what still has to be checked, before the film goes back to the hill itself. Spoken in Welsh, lip-synced; English and Spanish audio and cy/en/es subtitles available. Invented faces.
shots: 1. Title card held over a slow push-in on a closed archive box under a reading lamp; the title 'CEDWYN' and 'A tab.bot production' appear on screen.
2. Talking close-up of Nia, gloved, a single note card in her hand. Nia: “Before any deed, there was a name. Whose name, and whose hill?”

3. Wide establishing shot of the archive reading room; Nia pulls on cotton gloves and slides a stack of folders across to the Grandson, who sits down with his laptop. Nia: “Bore da. Gloves on before you touch anything. Before a single deed, we've got names. Just names, written in your family's research notes.” The Grandson: “Cedwyn. That's the word I keep tripping over. Cedwyn, Cwm-Cedwyn, Nant-Cedwyn, Ynys-Cedwyn. Then Cedfin, Cydfin, Cydwin. And Tŷ Mawr, the Great House.”

4. Overhead insert: Nia's gloved finger runs down a printed index sheet laid on the table. Nia: “This is the index. Six research leads. It shows where each name turns up, and which notes lean on which. Pull one out, you see what wobbles.”
5. Close-up on the Grandson, leaning in, hopeful. The Grandson: “So does it prove the Great House stood on Cedwyn land? That my family's roots there go back before any deed?”

6. Close-up on Nia, gentle but firm, taking off her glasses. Nia: “Not on its own. It proves the leads are catalogued. Whether the variants are one place, whether they mean Tŷ Mawr, and what any old lease meant for the land after 1877: those are the next checks.”

7. Insert: the Grandson lays a typed note card beside an unmarked sketch of a river bend. The Grandson: “Cwm-Cedwyn. A wooded dell on the Ely, between Leckwith and Llandough. My notes use it all the time.” Nia: “They do. But there's no source attached yet. We don't know when the name was first written, where its edges ran, or whether it ever touched Tŷ Mawr. Checking is still to do.”
8. Slow drift through Leckwith woods down to the River Ely in morning mist, birdsong, no people.

9. Insert: an empty labelled folder sleeve, nothing inside, held up to the lamp. The Grandson: “And Nant-Cedwyn. A brook running into the Ely near Leckwith.” Nia: “That one points to a primary document, and we haven't got it yet. So for now it shows us one thing: the family noted the name. Name, place, date, link to Tŷ Mawr: all still to be checked.”

10. Insert: a third note card set apart from the others, at the edge of the table. The Grandson: “Ynys-Cedwyn's the odd one out.” Nia: “Ynys-Cedwyn sits up where the Twrch meets the Tawe, a long way from here. The note ties it to Cedwyn Gawr, Cedwyn the Giant.”
11. Close-up on the Grandson, amused, half a laugh. The Grandson: “A giant. Lovely. Is there anything linking him to Llandough?”
12. Close-up on Nia, tapping the card once. Nia: “Not yet. No primary source, the place and the giant both waiting to be checked, and no link to Tŷ Mawr written down.”

13. Two-shot: the Grandson closes his laptop, Nia gathers the cards into one pile; the window light shifts toward the hills outside. The Grandson: “So the film starts with a name we can't pin down.” Nia: “It starts honest. A name, and a hill that came before it. Let's go and stand on the hill.”

en.intro: One unbroken scene on the same hilltop at Llandough, above the River Ely, in two moments four hundred years apart. First, about 200 BC: a late Iron Age family at their roundhouse bringing in the corn, minding the cattle on the marsh and preparing for winter. Then, about AD 200: a Romano-British farmer and his wife harvesting spelt on the same slope, with the stone house of the villa beyond the brow. Nobody speaks to the camera: they talk to each other, to a child, to the animals. They speak in modern Welsh, the nearest living language to their Brittonic, with English and Spanish subtitles. The faces are invented; no real person is shown.
shots: 1. Dawn, about 200 BC. A small homestead on the top of Llandough hill: thatched roundhouses with wattle-and-daub walls inside an earth bank, a raised granary on posts and a hurdle fold with a few small dark cattle. Smoke seeps up through the thatch and mist lifts off the reed marsh of the Ely far below. Caption: c. 200 BC, Llandough hill above the River Ely; spoken in modern Welsh, the nearest living language to theirs.
2. The roundhouse mother stands in the low doorway, the hearth glowing behind her. She looks up at the smoke and speaks to her husband: the weather should hold, so they can bring the corn in today.

3. The elder, grey-bearded in a brown wool cloak, stands in the field with a handful of cut ears and an iron sickle. He tells her to cut only the heads, high on the stalk, and leave the straw standing for the cattle to graze.
4. The harvest on the slope: the family cut the ear heads with small sickles and drop them into baskets while the wind runs through the standing grain.
5. Below them a boy drives the cattle up from the marsh with a hazel switch, the reeds swaying behind.
6. The mother watches him from the doorway and tells him the boy is bringing the cattle up off the marsh before the big tides come.
7. The elder, leaning on the wattle fence, answers quietly: last autumn the water came over the marsh in the night and they lost a calf.
8. Inside, at the upright loom, she keeps weaving as she answers: not this year. The pig is fat, the store is full, and the cloth is nearly ready for the little one's cloak.
9. Dusk. A skein of geese crosses the sky over the marsh; the elder watches them go, smoke curling from the roundhouse.
10. He crouches beside his small granddaughter, points at the geese and tells her the cold is coming, and to bring wood in by the door tonight.
11. Before dark the mother kneels at the spring below the homestead with a handful of the new corn: an offering to the water that has always kept them.

12. Time jump. Caption: c. AD 200, the same hill four hundred years on, a Romano-British farm at harvest. A late-summer field of spelt wheat, half reaped and stooked in rows, the river and marsh below; skylarks and wind.

13. A different family works the hill now. The farmer, a lean man in his thirties with cropped dark hair, in a wool tunic and cloak with a bronze brooch, rubs an ear of spelt between his palms and talks to his wife: the fires are already lit up at the stone house over the brow, the spelt is good this year and dry enough to thresh before the rain comes up the valley.

14. His wife, younger, in a linen headscarf and a madder-red wool dress, keeps binding a sheaf beside a basket holding bread and a glossy red bowl. Then thresh it quick, she answers: the quern is hungry and so are the children; fine red pots from far off, and they still eat the same porridge out of them.
15. The farmer swings his iron sickle through the spelt and lays the stalks down as she gathers and binds behind him.

16. She looks down the hill at grey cloud rising off the marsh and tells him to call the animals in. The geese are fat this year: one for the turn of the year, and one for his mother, or they will never hear the end of it.
17. He laughs and waves the geese off the sheaves: let them run, the hill is big enough for all of them.
18. Rain cloud rolls in as the ox cart, loaded with sheaves, creaks up the earth track and the geese scatter beside it. End card: Cedwyn, Scene 2, The hill before the records. A tab.bot production.

cy.intro: Un eiliad ar gopa bryn Llandochau, uwchben afon Elái, tua 650 OC. Mae mynach o'r fynachlog yn Llandochau yn arwain claddedigaeth ym mynwent y brodyr, lle mae'r beddau'n gorwedd mewn rhesi o'r gorllewin i'r dwyrain wrth ymyl safle hen adeilad Rhufeinig. Mae menyw o'r ardal yn sefyll wrth ochr y bedd. Does neb yn siarad â'r camera: mae'r mynach yn siarad â'r wraig farw ac â'r alarwraig, ac mae hithau'n ei ateb. Maen nhw'n siarad Cymraeg modern, yr iaith fyw agosaf at eu hiaith nhw, gydag isdeitlau Saesneg a Sbaeneg. Mae'r wynebau wedi'u dychmygu; does dim person go iawn i'w weld, ac mae gan yr olygfa hon ei chast ei hun, sy'n wahanol i'r golygfeydd cynharach.
shots: 1. Diwedd yr hydref ar gopa bryn Llandochau. Glaswellt gwlyb a drain gwynion; ymhell islaw, mae afon Elái yn ymdroelli trwy gorsydd cyrs tuag at aber niwlog. Capsiwn: c. 650, mynwent fynachaidd ar fryn Llandochau, uwchben afon Elái; y llefaru mewn Cymraeg modern, yr iaith fyw agosaf at eu hiaith nhw.

2. Mae gorymdaith angladdol fach yn croesi'r fynwent: mae dau frawd lleyg yn cario corff mewn amdo lliain plaen ar elor bren; mae'r mynach yn cerdded o'u blaen ac mae'r fenyw'n dilyn. Y tu hwnt, mae eglwys bren fach â tho gwellt. Capsiwn: o'r 5ed i'r 11eg ganrif, mae mynwent fynachaidd o'r Oesoedd Canol cynnar yn tyfu ar y bryn, wrth ymyl safle hen adeilad Rhufeinig (PX-03).
3. Caiff y corff yn ei amdo ei ollwng â rhaffau i fedd wedi'i dorri o'r gorllewin i'r dwyrain, a'r pen tua'r gorllewin, tra bo'r mynach yn sefyll wrth ben y bedd.
4. Mae'r mynach yn gadael i bridd syrthio i'r bedd ac yn siarad â'r wraig farw: pridd i'r pridd; gorwedd di yma gyda'r lleill, dy wyneb tua'r dwyrain, tua'r wawr.
5. Mae'r fenyw'n edrych ar hyd y rhesi o dwmpathau: mae cymaint ohonyn nhw, rhes ar ôl rhes, mwy bob gaeaf. Fydd hi'n unig yma?

6. Mae'r mynach yn troi tuag at yr eglwys fach: fydd hi byth yn unig; mae'r brodyr yn canu'r salmau yma bob cyfnos, uwchben afon Elái. Roedd yr eglwys yn hen pan ddaeth e, a bydd hi'n dal i sefyll ar ôl iddyn nhw fynd.
7. Mae rhaw bren yn taro yn erbyn carreg adeiladu sgwâr, hindreuliedig ym mhridd y bedd.
8. Mae'r fenyw'n cipedrych ar y garreg: o dan y dywarchen, yr hen gerrig; mae'r rhawiau'n dal i'w taro nhw.
9. Dyw'r mynach ddim yn poeni: cerrig y Rhufeiniaid ydyn nhw; mae'r Rhufeiniaid wedi hen fynd, a'r rhai sy'n aros, maen nhw yma. Mae'n cynnig ei law iddi: mae'r brodyr yn aros.

10. Cyfnos. Mae'r ddau'n cerdded ar draws pen y bryn tuag at yr eglwys, a golau gwan yn ei drws, tra bo'r corsydd islaw yn dal y golau olaf. Capsiwn: mae eglwys Sant Dochdwy, wrth ymyl y fferm ddiweddarach, yn sefyll lle mae archaeoleg yn lleoli mynachlog gynnar (CH-0001).

es.intro: Un momento en la cima de la colina de Llandough, sobre el río Ely, hacia el año 650 d. C. Un monje del monasterio de Llandough oficia un entierro en el cementerio de los hermanos, donde las tumbas se alinean en hileras de oeste a este junto al emplazamiento de un antiguo edificio romano. Una mujer de la zona está de pie junto a la tumba. Nadie le habla a la cámara: el monje le habla a la difunta y a la doliente, y ella le responde. Hablan en galés moderno, la lengua viva más cercana a la suya, con subtítulos en inglés y en español. Los rostros son inventados; no se muestra a ninguna persona real, y esta escena tiene su propio elenco, distinto del de las escenas anteriores.
shots: 1. Fines de otoño en la cima de la colina de Llandough. Pasto mojado y espinos; mucho más abajo, el río Ely serpentea entre juncales hacia un estuario brumoso. Rótulo: c. 650, cementerio monástico en la colina de Llandough, sobre el río Ely; hablado en galés moderno, la lengua viva más cercana a la suya.

2. Un pequeño cortejo fúnebre atraviesa el cementerio: dos hermanos legos cargan un cuerpo envuelto en una sencilla mortaja de lino sobre unas andas de madera; el monje va adelante y la mujer los sigue. Más allá se levanta una pequeña iglesia de madera con techo de paja. Rótulo: entre los siglos V y XI, en la colina crece un cementerio monástico altomedieval, junto al emplazamiento de un antiguo edificio romano (PX-03).
3. El cuerpo amortajado baja con sogas a una fosa excavada de oeste a este, con la cabeza hacia el oeste, mientras el monje se ubica en la cabecera de la tumba.
4. El monje deja caer tierra en la fosa y le habla a la difunta: tierra a la tierra; descansá acá con los demás, con la cara hacia el este, hacia el amanecer.
5. La mujer recorre con la mirada las hileras de túmulos: son tantos, hilera tras hilera, y cada invierno hay más. ¿Se sentirá sola acá?

6. El monje se vuelve hacia la pequeña iglesia: nunca sola; los hermanos cantan los salmos acá cada atardecer, sobre el río Ely. La iglesia ya era antigua cuando él llegó y va a seguir en pie cuando ellos ya no estén.
7. Una pala de madera golpea contra una piedra de construcción escuadrada y desgastada en la tierra de la fosa.
8. La mujer mira la piedra: bajo el pasto, las piedras viejas; las palas todavía chocan con ellas.
9. Al monje no le preocupa: son las piedras de los romanos; los romanos se fueron hace mucho, y los que se quedan están acá. Le ofrece la mano: los hermanos esperan.

10. Atardecer. Los dos cruzan la cima de la colina hacia la iglesia, con una tenue luz en la puerta, mientras los pantanos de abajo reciben la última luz del día. Rótulo: la iglesia de San Dochdwy, junto a la granja posterior, se levanta donde la arqueología sitúa un monasterio temprano (CH-0001).

en.intro: One moment on the crown of Llandough hill, above the River Ely, about AD 650. A monk of the monastery at Llandough leads a burial in the brothers' cemetery, where graves lie in rows from west to east beside the site of an older Roman building. A woman of the district stands at the graveside. Nobody speaks to the camera: the monk speaks to the dead woman and to the mourner, and she answers him. They speak in modern Welsh, the nearest living language to theirs, with English and Spanish subtitles. The faces are invented; no real person is shown, and this scene has its own cast, different from earlier scenes.
shots: 1. Late autumn on the crown of Llandough hill. Wet grass and hawthorn; far below, the Ely winds through reed marshes toward a hazy estuary. Caption: c. 650, monastic burial ground on Llandough hill, above the Ely; spoken in modern Welsh, the nearest living language to theirs.

2. A small funeral procession crosses the cemetery: two lay brothers carry a body in a plain linen shroud on a wooden bier; the monk walks ahead and the woman follows. A small thatched timber church stands beyond. Caption: from the 5th to the 11th century an early-medieval monastic cemetery grows on the hill, beside the site of an older Roman building (PX-03).
3. The shrouded body is lowered on ropes into a grave cut west to east, the head to the west, while the monk stands at the head of the grave.
4. The monk lets earth fall into the grave and speaks to the dead woman: earth to earth; lie here with the others, your face to the east, toward the dawn.
5. The woman looks along the rows of mounds: there are so many of them, row after row, more every winter. Will she be lonely here?
6. The monk turns toward the little church: never lonely; the brothers sing the psalms here every dusk, above the Ely. The church was old when he came and will stand after they are gone.
7. A wooden spade knocks against a squared, weathered building stone in the grave soil.
8. The woman glances at the stone: under the turf, the old stones; the spades still strike them.
9. The monk is unconcerned: they are the Romans' stones; the Romans are long gone, and those who stay are here. He offers her his hand: the brothers are waiting.

10. Dusk. The two walk across the hilltop toward the church, a faint light in its doorway, while the marshes below catch the last light. Caption: St Dochdwy's church, beside the later farm, stands where archaeology places an early monastery (CH-0001).
